title: An Aubry-André localized optical lattice clock
authors: Shuo Ma, Anke Stölzel, Bennett Christensen, Zhuoli Ding, Dhruva Ganapathy, Andrew Householder, Genyue Liu, Shimon Kolkowitz
abstract: Optical lattice clocks in space could improve satellite navigation systems and enable new tests of fundamental physics, including gravitational-wave detection and tests of relativity. In microgravity, atoms can tunnel to degenerate neighboring lattice sites, broadening the clock transition and limiting coherence times. We demonstrate Aubry-André localization in a bichromatic optical lattice formed by two magic-wavelength lasers, suppressing tunneling in a horizontal lattice clock emulating free fall. We recover a Fourier-limited clock Rabi spectrum and measure Ramsey coherence times of up to 2 s in shallow lattices, with up to 100-fold improvement over the delocalized regime. These results establish Aubry-André localization as a practical route to controlling tunneling in future space-based clocks, and open a path to operating terrestrial clocks at shallower lattice depths.
summary: This paper demonstrates that introducing a secondary, quasiperiodically modulated optical lattice can induce Aubry-André localization in an atomic clock system. This localization effectively suppresses detrimental atomic tunneling, which is a major source of decoherence in shallow lattices. The results show a significant recovery of the narrow, ideal clock transition spectrum and greatly extended coherence times, paving the way for next-generation space-based atomic clocks.
main_problem: Operating optical lattice clocks in space requires suppressing atomic tunneling between lattice sites to maintain coherence and achieve high precision.
main_result: Implementing Aubry-André localization in a bichromatic optical lattice restores a narrow, Fourier-limited clock spectrum and improves Ramsey coherence times by up to two orders of magnitude.
method: The authors model the system using the Aubry-André Hamiltonian, simulating Rabi spectra and coherence decay by varying lattice depths and introducing a secondary lattice modulation.
model_or_system: The system uses $^{87}	ext{Sr}$ atoms in a bichromatic optical lattice formed by two magic-wavelength lasers, emulating free fall. The physics is governed by the Aubry-André Hamiltonian, which describes the transition from a delocalized Bloch state to an exponentially localized state when a secondary lattice is introduced.
key_observables: Rabi spectra (measuring spectral narrowing), Ramsey coherence times ($	au$), and the on-resonance excitation fraction.
important_parameters: The ratio of lattice wavelengths ($ eta$), the modulation amplitude ($\Delta$), and the lattice depths ($U_{813}, U_{497}$).
main_assumptions: The AA Hamiltonian is derived by perturbatively projecting the secondary lattice modulation onto the lowest band of the primary lattice. The analysis also considers the regime where the secondary lattice acts as a weak modulation.
figures_summary: Figures show the transition of Rabi spectra from broadened, tunneling-limited spectra to narrow, Fourier-limited spectra upon applying AA localization. Other figures detail the temperature dependence of motional line pulling shifts.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of tunneling in space-based clocks. It then introduces and models the AA localization technique using a bichromatic lattice. The core of the work involves demonstrating the recovery of narrow spectral features and long coherence times by analyzing Rabi spectra and coherence decay rates.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally verifiable mechanism (AA localization) to control quantum coherence in a highly sensitive quantum sensor platform (optical lattice clocks), bridging condensed matter localization physics with precision measurement.
